result: Phylogeographic modeling indicates that bearded manakin speciation occurred in sympatry, with ancestral ranges overlapping 49-73% between golden-collared and the common ancestor of white-collared and orange-collared manakins. Modern species are mostly allopatric, suggesting geographic isolation followed rather than preceded diversification.
evaluation: Claims C13-C17, C67, C69-C70, and C72 are supported by phylogeographic modeling data shown in Figure 1. The methodology for reconstructing ancestral ranges is described in detail, using 12 geographic index points and MCMC sampling. The >25% overlap threshold for sympatric speciation is appropriately cited (C15). The inference that isolation followed diversification (C17) is logically sound given ancestral sympatry and current allopatry.

result: Evidence from hybridization studies and genomic analyses supports that mechanisms other than geographic isolation drove rapid speciation in bearded manakins. Golden-collared and white-collared manakins hybridize in Panama, with high introgression rates and genetic differentiation consistent with reproductive isolation following adaptive divergence.
evaluation: Claims C18-C22, C68, and C79 are supported by multiple citations to prior genomic and hybridization studies (Parsons et al., 1993; McDonald et al., 2001; Parchman et al., 2013). The inference that assortative mating facilitated rapid speciation (C68) is appropriately supported by theoretical citations and the phylogeographic evidence of sympatric speciation. The logic connecting hybridization evidence to non-geographic mechanisms is sound.

result: Roll-snap display speed diverged significantly among bearded manakin species, with golden-collared manakins producing the fastest displays (58.4 Hz) and orange-collared the slowest, while display length remained statistically indistinguishable across species. This divergence occurred in ancestrally sympatric taxa during speciation.
evaluation: Claims C23-C25, C29-C30, C71, and C73 are well-supported by acoustic data from 119 recordings analyzed with appropriate statistical methods (LMM with post-hoc testing, Figure 2). Sample sizes are adequate (Table 1), and the finding of speed divergence without length divergence is clearly demonstrated (F3,146=9.203, p<0.0001 for speed; F3,153=0.229, p=0.876 for length). The temporal correlation with speciation (C71, C73) is supported by phylogeographic and acoustic data.

result: Divergent roll-snap speeds may reinforce conspecific mate preference and support assortative mating during sympatric speciation, with sexual selection potentially driving phenotypic displacement in this mate choice trait. Alternative mechanisms for display divergence are also considered.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32, C2, C4, C68, C75-C77, and C85 involve substantial inference about the role of sexual selection and female preferences in speciation. While the logic is sound and supported by theoretical citations, direct evidence that females attend to roll-snap speed differences is lacking (C31 acknowledges this). The claim that roll-snap speed is sexually selected (C11) is inferred from studies on other displays. Alternative hypotheses (C75-C76) are appropriately presented, but the causal link between display divergence and assortative mating remains speculative without behavioral experiments.

result: Quantile regression analysis reveals a speed-endurance trade-off in golden-collared and white-collared manakins at the upper performance bounds (τ=0.9), but not in white-bearded or orange-collared manakins. The trade-off is steeper and affects more individuals (top 80%) in golden-collared manakins compared to white-collared manakins (top 20%), indicating differential constraints across species.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 and C81 are supported by quantile regression analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2. The statistical approach is appropriate for detecting performance trade-offs, with significant negative slopes at τ=0.9 for golden-collared (t=-4.03, p<0.001) and white-collared (t=-2.76, p=0.007) manakins. The comparison of slope steepness (F1,230=22.1, p=0.001) and the extent of the trade-off across quantiles is well-documented. The interpretation that constraints are differential across species is justified by the data.

result: Golden-collared manakins have a significantly faster scapulohumeralis caudalis (SH) muscle than white-collared manakins, with greater half-relaxation frequency (F1,49=79.8, p<0.001), corresponding to their faster roll-snap displays.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 and C82 are supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 4c-d. The methodology is well-described, with appropriate sample sizes (n=3-5 for golden-collared, n=3 for white-collared). Statistical comparison of four-parameter logistic models (F3,49=15.2, p<0.001) and half-relaxation frequencies is appropriate. The correspondence between muscle speed and display speed is clearly demonstrated, though the sample size for white-collared manakins is at the lower limit.

result: The golden-collared manakin SH muscle exhibits 'rapid fatigue' when stimulated at ≥80 Hz, with percent relaxation declining from 75-100% to 20-50% across stimulation trains. This phenomenon is absent in white-collared manakins, representing a severe speed-endurance trade-off.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51, C54, and C3 are supported by in situ muscle recording data shown in Figure 5a-b and Table 3. Statistical analysis demonstrates significant declines in percent relaxation for golden-collared manakins at 80 Hz (F1,12=18.7, p=0.005), 90 Hz (F1,12=33.9, p<0.001), and 100 Hz (F1,12=22.8, p=0.003), while white-collared manakins show no such decline. The regression analysis showing performance decline with frequency (F1,6=27.7, p=0.004, R²=0.82) is robust.

result: The speed-endurance trade-off in golden-collared manakins manifests at approximately 60 Hz, which corresponds closely to their average roll-snap speed of 58.4 Hz. This suggests sexual selection has driven the display to the muscle's performance limit, with males producing shorter displays at speeds ≥60 Hz.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58, C83, C86-C87 are supported by the convergence of muscle performance data (Figure 5c) and acoustic data (Figure 2a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The correspondence between the threshold where the 95% CI crosses zero (~60 Hz) and average display speed (58.4 Hz) is compelling. The finding that males produce shorter displays at ≥60 Hz (β=-4.32, F1,119=46.7, p<0.001) provides additional support. However, the inference that this represents the absolute performance limit requires caution, as further muscle modifications might be possible.

result: The 'rapid fatigue' in golden-collared manakins results from decreased relaxation capacity rather than changes in contraction/relaxation timing. This may be linked to constraints on calcium handling mechanisms, suggesting evolutionary mismatch between different components of muscle machinery.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by data in Figure 6 showing no significant changes in contraction/relaxation timing (pmin=0.20). However, claims C61, C63-C64 about calcium handling mechanisms are speculative, appropriately acknowledged by the authors with phrases like 'may be linked' and 'likely require.' While the inference is reasonable given the role of calcium in muscle relaxation (supported by citations), direct evidence for calcium handling limitations is absent. The claim of evolutionary mismatch (C63) is plausible but unproven.

result: The observed 'rapid fatigue' differs from standard muscle fatigue in timescale (fractions of a second vs. longer periods) but qualifies as a form of endurance. This mechanism differs from typical speed-endurance trade-offs associated with fiber type composition.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C65-C66 are supported by appropriate citations defining standard muscle fatigue (Wilson et al., 2002; Allen et al., 2008) and typical mechanisms of speed-endurance trade-offs (Rivero et al., 1993; Komi, 1984). The distinction between 'rapid fatigue' and standard fatigue is clearly articulated and justified by the timescale differences. The classification of resistance to rapid fatigue as a form of endurance is logically sound given the definition of endurance as the ability to resist fatigue.

result: The study demonstrates that muscle physiology influences how divergent selection drives phenotypic evolution during speciation with gene flow, with physiological design creating the landscape for phenotypic evolution and contributing to species divergence.
evaluation: Claims C84, C90-C91 represent appropriate synthesis of the study's findings. The integration of phylogeographic, behavioral, and physiological data provides strong support for the role of muscle constraints in shaping display evolution during sympatric speciation. However, these are broad conceptual claims that summarize the work rather than presenting new specific findings. The evidence is compelling within the bearded manakin system but generalization to other systems requires caution.

result: Background claims establish the bearded manakin system: four species diverged ~300,000 years ago, males produce roll-snap displays by rapidly hitting wings together, signal speed is important in courtship, females prefer faster displays in related behaviors, and the SH muscle actuates the display while facing speed-endurance trade-offs.
evaluation: Claims C5-C12, C28, C42-C45 are background information supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These establish the study system and theoretical framework. The phylogenetic timing (C5) and taxonomy (C6) are from Brumfield et al., 2008 and Tello et al., 2009. The biomechanics of the roll-snap (C7, C42-C43) and muscle function (C44-C45) are from prior studies by the authors and others. Female preferences (C10) are from Barske et al., 2011, though for other displays, not the roll-snap itself.

result: General evolutionary principles and context: phenotypes evolve under directional selection until impeded by rate-limiting mechanisms; plumage has also diverged in manakins due to sexual selection, though dichromatism alone may not facilitate sympatric speciation.
evaluation: Claims C62, C88-C89 provide theoretical context and acknowledge other divergent traits. C62 is a general principle of evolutionary biology supported by the data. C88-C89 are appropriately cited (McDonald et al., 2001; Cooney et al., 2017) and acknowledge that multiple traits have diverged, though the authors argue display behavior may be more important for sympatric speciation than plumage alone.

result: Additional observations: mean speed differences are small (<5 Hz) but reflect larger differences at upper performance ranges; orange-collared manakins don't hybridize with golden-collared manakins; other unmeasured display aspects may also support divergence.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by acoustic data analysis. C78 is based on absence of reported hybridization in the literature. C80 appropriately acknowledges study limitations and suggests future work on other display parameters (amplitude, modulation). These are minor supporting observations and appropriate caveats.
